extracted.intended_audience: educated lay readers with some mathematical background and professional mathematicians
extracted.subtask_description: A book-length, essay-style exploration of what mathematics is, how it is created and communicated, who practices it, and how it fits into culture — aimed at both educated lay readers and practicing mathematicians.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematics as the science of quantity and space
rubrics_metrics.description: Naive definition: mathematics is the science of quantity and space (expanded to include symbolism relating to quantity and space).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical basis: arithmetic (numbers and operations) and geometry (spatial measurement and aesthetic/spatial facts such as tilings and triangle/diagonal facts). Examples given (tiling with equilateral triangles/hexagons, parallelogram diagonals, medians of a triangle). This serves as a useful starting definition but is acknowledged as incomplete for modern mathematics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematics as a deductive science (proof-centered)
rubrics_metrics.description: Peirce's formulation: 'mathematics is the science of making necessary conclusions.' Euclidean geometry presented as the first model of a formalized deductive system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasizes assumption → deduction → conclusion pattern; proof is presented as the characteristic methodology (Euclid as exemplar). Examples and analogies (Sherlock Holmes/detection as 'exact science') illustrate that the deductive pattern, not specific content, defines the form. The role of proof in teaching (geometry) is highlighted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form over content: any subject with deductive structure can be mathematics
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematics could be 'about' anything as long as it is a subject that exhibits the pattern of assumption-deduction-conclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by analogy that criminal detection might be treated like a mathematical discipline because it follows the deductive pattern. The point is that the pattern of reasoning, rather than specific topics (quantity/space), can define mathematics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discovery vs. proof — the methodological reality
rubrics_metrics.description: The working mathematician's activity is often 'a tangle of guesswork, analogy, wishful thinking and frustration,' while proof is 'more often than not a way of making sure that our minds are not playing tricks.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This distinguishes the creative, heuristic phase (conjecturing, analogizing) from the formal phase of proving; it cautions against the misleading view that mathematics is primarily about theorem statements and proofs as the whole of the discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions and foundational schools are plural and change over time
rubrics_metrics.description: Different generations and schools formulate differing definitions (examples: logicists, formalists, constructivists); each generation modifies and amplifies the definition of mathematics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Warns readers that no single static definition will be definitive; the book intends to examine alternate formulations. Expect historical and philosophical plurality rather than a single dogma.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ontology/location of mathematics (where mathematics 'is')
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematics exists on the printed page, in people's minds, on taped lectures, in computer memories and printed circuits, and perhaps (debatedly) 'eternally' and independently of actualization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Raises questions about Platonism vs. other views: should mathematical facts be located in physical artifacts (shadows, genetic arrangements, machines) or in an abstract realm? Cites Ayer's remark on philosophy's dream 'to agree on a criterion for deciding what there is.' Examples: lamp-shade parabola, sunflower spirals, Stonehenge; no definitive resolution is offered here.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical community structure and the social institutions sustaining mathematics
rubrics_metrics.description: Modern mathematics is an international, unified enterprise with publications, national/international meetings, exchanges, and institutional sponsorship (universities, corporations, government).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives concrete indicators: membership numbers (AMS, MAA, SIAM), number of technical journals (~1600), and funding (e.g., federal spending). Notes exceptions (wartime secrecy, cryptography). Emphasizes openness, communication, and institutional support as necessary conditions for high-quality research and transmission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Auxiliary tools and instruments required for mathematics
rubrics_metrics.description: Although thought-experiments are important, mathematics requires instruments of writing, recording, and duplication; specific instruments (ruler and compass) are built into Euclidean axioms; computers, slide rules, cash registers are mathematical machines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical note: transmission moved from oral tradition to written records, scribal replication, printing. Theoretical work still depends on external media (blackboard, books, computers). The ruler-and-compass tradition is cited as an example of tools incorporated into mathematical axioms and methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pedagogical emphasis: written/formal work versus spoken exposition
rubrics_metrics.description: In ordinary mathematics teaching, the main work is written (blackboard/written proofs); spoken words are secondary and important only insofar as they communicate or clarify the written content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrast drawn with a foundations course that asks to 'talk about' mathematics rather than 'do' it: different expectations and methods. Highlights a practical classroom criterion: success is measured by completed written problems/theorems rather than by spoken exposition alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematics as a human activity accessible at multiple levels
rubrics_metrics.description: Everyone does some mathematics (market purchases, measurements, decorative patterns); a smaller professional community creates and transmits new mathematics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrates inclusiveness: quotidian arithmetic and pattern use versus specialized research-level mathematics. Historical examples of varied practitioners (archbishop, fencing master, lawyer, physician) demonstrate that mathematicians have come from diverse walks of life; modern practice is concentrated but still intersects many professions (physics, engineering, computer science).
